stem: A parent asks whether aspirin should be given to a child who has influenza-like symptoms. Which teaching is appropriate?

options.A: Use aspirin routinely for viral fever because Reye syndrome is associated with bacterial infections rather than viral illness.
options.B: Delay aspirin until the viral fever has lasted at least 24 hours because duration of fever determines whether Reye syndrome can occur.
options.C: Combine aspirin with acetaminophen during viral illness because concurrent acetaminophen prevents the aspirin-associated Reye risk.
options.D: Do not give aspirin to a child or teenager who has or is recovering from flu-like illness unless a clinician specifically directs its use.

rationale: The current DailyMed aspirin 325-mg OTC label includes a Reye-syndrome warning stating that children and teenagers who have or are recovering from chickenpox or flu-like symptoms should not use the product. Therefore D is correct and preserves the clinician-directed exception used in patient teaching. A reverses the viral-illness association, B invents a fever-duration threshold, and C falsely implies acetaminophen eliminates the aspirin-associated Reye warning.
educational_objective: Teach caregivers not to give aspirin to children or teenagers with or recovering from flu-like illness or chickenpox unless specifically directed by a clinician because of the Reye-syndrome warning.

source_claim_supported: Aspirin should not be given to children or teenagers with or recovering from flu-like symptoms or chickenpox because of the labeled Reye-syndrome warning unless clinician-directed use is specifically indicated.

source_original.stem: A parent asks whether aspirin should be given to a child who has influenza-like symptoms. Which teaching is appropriate?

options.A: Use aspirin routinely for viral fever because Reye syndrome is associated with bacterial infections rather than viral illness.
options.B: Delay aspirin until the viral fever has lasted at least 24 hours because duration of fever determines whether Reye syndrome can occur.
options.C: Combine aspirin with acetaminophen during viral illness because concurrent acetaminophen prevents the aspirin-associated Reye risk.
options.D: Avoid aspirin during a child or teenager’s viral illness unless a clinician specifically directs its use because of the Reye-syndrome association.

source_original.rationale: Aspirin labeling warns that children and teenagers who have or are recovering from chickenpox or flu-like symptoms should not use aspirin because of the association with Reye syndrome unless directed by a clinician.
source_original.source_detail: Warnings > Reye’s syndrome. DailyMed label currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Overview of Content — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12: medication administration, controlled substances, adverse effects/interactions, monitoring and teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the aspirin/Reye-syndrome construct and key D. Updated the label currentness to the June 25, 2026 DailyMed version and tightened D to the exact labeled population—children/teenagers who have or are recovering from flu-like illness—without adding an unsupported fever-duration or drug-combination rule.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Aspirin use during pediatric viral illness / Reye syndrome warning
audit_findings.source_authority: Current DailyMed official aspirin OTC label; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.exact_locator: DailyMed Warnings > Reye’s syndrome; NCSBN printed p.38 Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies rendered and verified
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item uses the exact labeled Reye-syndrome warning population and avoids inventing a fever-duration threshold, bacterial-only association, or protective effect from concurrent acetaminophen.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because the warning is specifically tied to chickenpox/flu-like viral illness, not bacterial infection only.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because the label does not make aspirin safety depend on 24 hours of fever duration.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because acetaminophen does not negate the labeled aspirin/Reye warning.
distractor_audit.D: Correct and directly supported by the current DailyMed warning.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D follows the labeled warning without adding an unsupported timing or combination strategy.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are caregiver medication-teaching statements about aspirin during the same viral illness context.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication contraindications/warnings, adverse-effect prevention and teaching.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked the current DailyMed label date and Reye warning, the rendered NCSBN pharmacology page, all four options, rationale, objective, ambiguity and cueing. D remained uniquely correct.
